args.rationale: This 38-year-old woman most likely has primary adrenal insufficiency from bilateral tuberculous adrenalitis. CT shows calcified bilateral adrenal nodules and old lung and pleural TB lesions (imaging_007). The left adrenal biopsy showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, but acid-fast and silver stains were negative (procedure_result_009). She has mild pigmentation over her finger joints and knees (hpi_001, physical_exam_003). She was hospitalized for a chest opacity 5 years ago but was never diagnosed with or treated for TB (pmh_002). The source did not report her vital signs, electrolytes, cortisol, ACTH, renin/aldosterone or TB blood test. The hydrocortisone and HRZE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) orders were recorded, but the system did not check their safety. Rifampicin speeds up cortisol breakdown, which can bring on an adrenal crisis. Admitting her lets us watch her closely while treatment starts, check liver tests and electrolytes, and adjust her hydrocortisone dose.
args.followup_or_handoff: Handoff to inpatient endocrinology and infectious disease. 1) Document baseline vital signs, including lying and standing blood pressure. 2) Before HRZE starts, check sodium, potassium, glucose, creatinine, liver tests, uric acid, HIV and hepatitis serology, visual acuity and color vision. Record weight so the fixed-dose tablets are dosed by weight band. 3) Draw cortisol, ACTH, and renin/aldosterone. If cortisol can't be drawn before hydrocortisone is given, switch to dexamethasone or hold a dose so the test isn't falsified. Add fludrocortisone 0.05–0.1 mg daily if renin is high or she has low sodium or high potassium. 4) Screen for active TB: sputum AFB smear, culture and PCR, and a chest CT review. Ask pathology to run TB PCR and mycobacterial culture on the biopsy tissue and to rule out fungal infection, sarcoidosis and cancer. 5) Raise hydrocortisone to about 30–40 mg/day while she is on rifampicin. Teach her sick-day rules and injectable hydrocortisone, and give her a steroid emergency card or bracelet. 6) Before discharge, arrange endocrinology follow-up in 2–4 weeks and TB clinic follow-up with monthly liver tests. Note that adrenal function rarely recovers after treatment.
